4. The respondent No. 1 is the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Land. The respondent No. 2 is the Divisional Commissioner of Dhaka Division who passed the final order of acquisition for inclusion of the petitioner company's land. Respondent No. 3 is the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka who initiated the acquisition proceedings being LA Case No. 2/2011-2012, the respondent No. 4 is the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA), Dhaka and the respondent No. 5 is the Land Acquisition Officer(s), Dhaka who issued various notices of the said LA Case from the office the respondent No. 3. 

 5. The petitioners in this Writ Petition have challenged the propriety and legality for inclusion/acquisition of the petitioner company's 123 decimals of land situated at Mouza-Zamur and Mouza-Zamur Muchipara comprising RS Khatian Nos. 295, 110, 114, 107 and R.S. Dag Nos. 304, 49, 50 & 51 under Police Station-Savar, District-Dhaka in LA Case No. 2/2011-2012, initiated by the respondent Nos. 3 under the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. 

 11. When the petitioner company after doing all the needful wanted to start construction of factory building for its compliant garments in the said land, with utter shock and surprise came to know that the respondent No. 3 initiated proceedings to acquire the petitioners land for the purpose of transferring Police Line Mill barrack from Dhaka to Savar. As soon as the petitioner company came to know about the said acquisition proceedings being LA Case No. 2/2011-2012, the concerned officials of the petitioner company rushed to the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka (respondent No. 3) and enquired into the matter. During such enquiry, it was detected that a notice under section 3 of Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (hereinafter also referred to as the said Ordinance) was issued to various persons including the previous record-holders of the petitioners land, but no notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance was issued to the petitioner company. Thus, the concerned person of the petitioner company immediately filed Preliminary Objection to the office of respondent No. 3. 

 12. Having regard to the objections raised by the petitioner company, the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 vide letter dated 17-8-2011 (process No. 51 dated 18-8-2011) served notice to the Managing Director of the petitioner company and asked him to submit relevant title deeds and records of rights in support of its title and fixed a date on 24-8-2011 at 10-00 am for submitting the same (Annexure G). In order to protect the land from the impugned acquisition proceedings initiated by the respondent No. 3, the petitioner company gave a representation on 13-8-2011 in the form of Written Objection with reasonable details. The petitioner company also made representation to the Secretary, Ministry of Land and the Hon'ble State Minister for Law, Justice & Parliamentary Affairs Government of Bangladesh for excluding the land of the petitioner company from the proposed acquisition of land (Annexure H series). Petitioner company also submitted all its title deeds and record of rights to the office of the respondent No. 3 on 24-8-2011. But the respondents did not take any initiate in this regard. 

 15. Mr M Sakhawat Hossain, (the petitioner No. 2) learned Advocate-in-person submits that as per section 4' of Sub-section (2) of the said Ordinance every objection under section 4 of Sub-section (1) shall be made to the Deputy Commissioner (i.e. respondent No. 3) in writing and the respondent No. 3 shall give the Objector an opportunity of being heard either in person or by an agent and shall, after hearing all such objections and after making such further enquiry, if any, as he thinks necessary, prepare report containing his opinion on the objections. Although serious objection was raised by the petitioner company to the respondent No. 3 regarding the proposed acquisition proceedings vides its letter dated 13-8-2011 but the respondent No. 3 did not give the petitioner company any opportunity of being heard either in person or by an agent in gross violation of section 4 of sub-section (2) of the said Ordinance. When the Managing Director of the petitioner company submitted the relevant title deeds and records of rights to the office of the respondent No. 3 on 24-8-2011 he had also submitted a written objection in the Prescribed Form and these are lying with the office of the respondent Nos. 3 and 4. Petitioner company also vide its letter dated 14-12-2011 requested the respondent No. 3 to give a hearing on the basis of its objection by enclosing therewith the said letter of objection dated 13-8-2011. 

 16. As per the said Ordinance, respondent No. 3 (i.e the Deputy Commissioner), after preparing report in terms of section 4, sub-section (2), if the property exceeds 50 standard bighas of land shall submit the report of the proceedings held by him together with his report for the decision of the Government and if the property does not exceed 50 bighas of land shall submit the record of the proceedings held by him together with his report for the decision of the Divisional Commissioner. Section 5 of the said Ordinance provides that the Government or as the case may be, the Divisional Commissioner after considering the report submitted by the Deputy Commissioner under section 4, sub-section (3) of the said Ordinance shall make a decision about the acquisition of the property and such decision of the Government or as the case may be, the Divisional Commissioner shall be final. 

 17. Since the property proposed to be acquired does not exceed 50 standard bighas of land and, as such, the Deputy Commissioner (i.e. respondent No. 3) vide Order No. 8 dated 26-8-2011 submitted his report to the Divisional Commissioner (i.e. respondent No. 4) for final decision of the proposed acquisition. The said Order No. 8 dated 26-9-2011 was signed by the respondent No. 3 on 28-9-2011. The report of the respondent No. 3 as per Order No. 8 dated 26-9-2011 is as follows:— 

 18. The Divisional Commissioner after receiving the report from the respondent No. 3 passed a final decision for acquisition of the land on 1-12-2011 in the following terms:— 

 19. As per Order No. 8 dated 26-9-2011, respondent No. 3 has initially rejected the objection raised by the Objector Nos. 1, 2 and 4 and allowed the objection raised by the Objector No. 3 in the said acquisition proceeding. Subsequently, the respondent No. 3 realized that he did not have the authority to accept or reject any such application but he can recommend the same to the Divisional Commissioner; hence without disposing of the objection raised by the Objector Nos. 1-4, he has recommended his observation to the Divisional Commissioner. In addition to the said 4 (four) Objectors, there were as many as additional 16 objectors who are also the owners in the proposed acquisition of lands. But their objections were not taken into consideration as the said objections allegedly have been filed after the expiry of the time-frame as mentioned in the said Ordinance. 

 20. Referring to the said Order No. 8 dated 26-9-2011 Mr M. Sakhawat Hossain further submits that the respondent No. 3 at the time of preparing his report in terms of section 4, sub-section (3) of the said Ordinance, he without considering and without mentioning that the land of the petitioner company as land for the industrial purpose submitted his report to the Divisional Commissioner (respondent No. 2). The respondent No. 3 has submitted his report in respect of Objector No. 3 (Rakib Apparels Ltd. represented by Mr Md Masuk Alam) stating, inter alia, that the land belongs to the Objector No. 3 was in the sideline of the proposed acquisition and it is a part of a factory. The Objector No. 3 purchased the adjacent land of the petitioner company for their garments factory, namely, Rakib Apparels Ltd. and when notice under section 3 was issued for the proposed acquisition there was no sign of any factory in the land of the objector No. 3 but in order to substantiate the report of the respondent No. 3, the objector No. 3 now in full swing started construction in their land for their garments factory. 

 22. Mr M Sakhawat Hossain further submits that the land of the Objector No. 3 being RS Plot No. 65 of Mouza-Tatul Zora is the adjacent land of the petitioner company being RS Plot No. 304 of Mouza-Zamur, while the land of RS Plot No. 49, 50 and 51 belongs to petitioner company of Mouza-Zamur Muchipara are the adjacent land of the aforesaid Plot No. 304, which are situated as a single pice of land. As per the acquisition map said RS Plot No. 65 of Mouza -Tatuljuhara of the Objector No. 3 is situated in the middle portion of the proposed acquired land, while the land belongs to the petitioner company being R.S Plot No. 49, 50 and 51 of Mouza-Zamur Muchipara and RS Plot No. 304 of Mouza-Tatul Zora are situated on the side line of the purposed acquisition. 

 24. On the basis of the said report dated 26-8-2011 (signed by the respondent No. 3 on 28-9- 2011) the Divisional Commissioner (i.e. respondent No. 2) accorded its final decision for acquisition of the land for 10.16 acres. From the Order No. 9 dated 1-12-2011 passed by the Divisional Commissioner that actual land proposed to be acquired was 10.56 acres but when the decision was passed by the Divisional Commissioner the acquisition was modified for an area of 10.16 acres, after allowing the objection of the Objector No. 3 i.e. upon excluding the land of Rakib Apparels Ltd. But no explanation was given as to why the Objection of the Objector No. 3 (Rakib Apparels Ltd. represented by Mr Md Masuk Alam) was allowed and why objection raised by the petitioner company (Aman Knittings Ltd.) was disallowed since both the objections were for saving industrial lands. Mr M Sakhawat Hossain submits that it is a clear case of discrimination and, as such, inclusion of the petitioner land in the said L.A case should be set aside through the judicial review of this Hon'ble Court. 

 25. Mr M Sakhawat Hossain submits that if the respondent No. 3 would have prepared a complete report and forwarded the same to the respondent No. 2 for his final decision, as per section 5 of the said Ordinance then it is likely that the objection of the petitioner company would have been allowed in the same manner as objection of the Objector No. 3 was allowed by the Divisional Commissioner. In fact, the Divisional Commissioner did not aware of the situation that the property of the petitioner company belongs to a Company and the said land was purchased by the petitioner company for the purpose of establishing a Compliant Garment Industry. It is a clear case of discrimination and arbitrary exercise of power by the respondents. Moreover, the arbitrary, discriminatory and malafide acts are always said to have been passed, without lawful authority, and, as such, Mr M Sakhawat Hossain submits that the land of the petitioner company should be excluded from the said. The land of the petitioner company should not be taken away by arbitrary and discriminatory exercise of powers by the respondents. The order passed by the respondent No. 2 dated 1-12-2011 regarding final acquisition of the petitioners land is ex-facie illegal, because he cannot pass a final order on the basis of an incomplete report forwarded by the respondent No.3. 

 26. Mr M Sakhawat Hossain further submits that while preparing the report, respondent No. 3 totally failed to consider the direction Nos. 12 and 25 of the Underlying Guidelines and Directions stipulated in the Land Acquisition Manual 1997, which was issued and published by the Ministry of Land on 15-10-2003 for acquisition of land under the said Ordinance. For ready reference, Direction No. 12 and Direction No, 25 are reproduced below for ready reference: 

 27. Mr M Sakhawat Hossain further submits that the respondent Nos. 3 and 4 submitted an incomplete report to the respondent No. 2 for his final decision without having considered the said Underlying Guidelines and Directions No. 12 and 25 and thereby totally suppressed and ignored the fact that the land belongs to the petitioner company was purchase& for establishing a garments industry, which generates employment and earns invaluable foreign currency for the country. The incomplete report of the respondent Nos. 3 and 4, without considering the above Direction Nos. 12 and 25 is ex-facie illegal and arbitrary and, as such, the land of the petitioner company should be excluded from the present acquisition process. 

 28. Mr M Sakhawat Hossain next contends that when the Ministry of Land issued any principle or policy for guiding the exercise of the discretion by the respondent No. 2 in the matter of selection or classification for acquisition of land, then such discretion is no longer unfettered and cannot be exercised arbitrarily and any exercise of discretion contrary to such policy or guidelines can be struck down in order to avoid discrimination between persons or things similarly situated. On this count the petitioners relied on the decisions of the following cases: 

 29. In the case of Jibendra Kishore vs East Pakistan, (1957) 9 DLR (SC) 21, the law provided for wholesale acquisition of the rent-receiving interest and permitted the government to acquire it at a time or part by part was held non - discriminatory in nature but in an obiter dicta of this case it was held "that even where the law itself is fair on its face and impartial in appearance, if it is applied and administered with an evil eye and unequal hand, the action taken under it will not be sustained by a Court." 

 33. He further submits that final order of acquisition dated 1-12-2011 passed by the respondent No. 2 (Divisional Commissioner) is not a speaking order. Moreover, the respondent No. 2 has not given any reason whatsoever as to why the land of the objector No. 3. (Rakib Apparels Ltd. represented by Mr Md Masuk Alam) should be excluded and why the land of the petitioner company (Arran Knittings Ltd.) should be included in the proposed acquisition. 

 (ii) State of West Bengal vs Atul Krishna Shaw, AIR 1990, 2205. 

 36. For non-speaking order in State of West Bengal vs Atul Krishna Shaw, AIR 1990 SC 2205 it was held that 

 "giving of reasons is an essential element of administration of justice. A right to reason is, therefore, an indispensible part of sound system of judicial review. Reasoned decision is not only for the purpose of showing that the citizen is receiving justice, but also a valid discipline for the Tribunal itself. Therefore, statement of reasons is one of the essentials of justice." 

 37. In Zahir Sheikh vs Md Yakub Ali, 43 DLR 168 it was held that the court's order cannot be said to be speaking order when it does not contain the reasoning. So, administrative order passed without any reasoning is a non-speaking order and, as such, final acquisition order should be set aside through the judicial review of this Hon'ble Court. 

 18. Acquisition of land for industrial areas:— 

 If any land situated in an area declared under section 17 to be an industrial area is required for any industrial project approved under section 11, such land shall be deemed to be required for public purpose and it may be requisitioned or acquired for such purpose under the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (11 of 1982). 

 42. Mr Md Mokleshur Rahman, learned Deputy Attorney-General and learned Assistant Attorney General Mr Titus Hillol Rema appearing on behalf of respondent No. 3 submit that the acquisition proceeding was done for greater public interest with the approval of Central Land Acquisition Committee. The petitioner has filed the objection after the expiry of the statutory period of time and thus, it deserves no consideration. Land in question is necessary for the proposed purpose for greater public interest. The said acquisition bid of the respondents is not violative of Articles 27, 31, 40 and 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as such the learned Deputy Attorney General submits that the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 45. As per the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 Government is authorized to acquire any land if it is needed for public purpose or in the public by issuing a notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance. Section 4 of the said Ordinance authorizes the citizen to give objections to any proposed acquisition. It appears from Annexure G that the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 recognized the objection of the petitioner company vide letter dated 17-8-2011 (process No. 51 dated 18-8-2011) and from Annexure H and I series it further appears that the petitioner company filed further written objection to the respondent No. 3 on 13-8-2011 long before passing the final order dated 1-12-2011 passed by the Divisional Commissioner (i.e. respondent No. 2). Section 5 of the said Ordinance provides that the Government or as the case may be, the Divisional Commissioner  after considering the report submitted by the Deputy Commissioner under section 4 sub-section (3) of the said Ordinance shall make a decision and such decision of the Government or as the case may be, the Divisional Commissioner shall be final. 

 46. The said Ordinance provides discretionary power to the Government/Divisional Commissioner to acquire the land of the petitioners but at the same time Government provides principles and policies for guiding the exercise of discretion in the matter of selection or classification. At the time of serving the proposed acquisition of land by Government consideration must be given as to whether any business of any citizen will be affected and whether the price of the land is low or high for any proposed acquisition. Since, the Ministry of Land issued such policy or guideline for exercise of discretion and, as such, this discretion is no longer unfettered and same cannot be exercised arbitrarily and any exercise of discretion contrary to such policy or guide-lines can be struck down. 

 47. It appears that on the basis of the report dated 26-8-2011 (signed by the respondent No. 3 on 28-9-2011) the Divisional Commissioner (i.e. respondent No. 2) gave the final decision for acquisition of the land for 10.16 acres. It appears from the Order No. 9 dated 1-12-2011 passed by the Divisional Commissioner that actual land proposed to be acquired was 10.56 acres but when the decision was passed by the Divisional Commissioner the acquisition was modified for an area of 10.16 acres, after allowing the objection of the Objector No. 3. But no explanation was given as to why the Objection of the Objector No. 3 was allowed and why objection raised by the petitioner company was disallowed when both the objections were for saving industrial lands. Hence we observe that it is case of discrimination and the decision is violative of Article 27 and 31 of the Constitution. 

 48. Moreover, final order of acquisition dated 1-12-2011 passed by the respondent No. 2 (Divisional Commissioner) is not a speaking order. The respondent No. 2 has not given any reason whatsoever as to why the land of the objector No. 3 (Rakib Apparels Ltd. represented by Mr Md Masuk Alam) should be excluded and why the land of the petitioner company (Aman Knittings Ltd.) should be included in the proposed acquisition. 

 49. An administrative order must be a reasoned one. Fairness and transparency of administrative decisions require to be recorded. The requirement of recording reasons by every quasi-judicial or even an administrative authority entrusted with the task of passing an order adversely against an individual and communication thereof to the affected persons is one of the recognized facets of the rules of natural justice and violation thereof has the effect of vitiating the order passed by the authority concerned. Hence we further observe that the final acquisition order dated 1-12-2011 passed by the Divisional Commissioner (respondent No. 2) was not reasoned one. We think that giving of reason is an essential element of administration of justice and it is a requirement of law. 

 50. Finally, we have gone through the proposed acquisition map and observed that total land proposed to be acquired is 10.16 acar and if the 1.23 acre (123 decimals) of land of the petitioners is excluded from the present acquisition the purpose of the government will not be frustrated.
